articles.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Pretreatment Evaluation and Follow-Up of Endometrial Cancer: 2026 Update.
articles.abstract: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States, and accurate pretreatment evaluation is essential for risk stratification, treatment planning, and detection of recurrent disease. This evidence-based review summarizes imaging recommendations for patients with established endometrial cancer undergoing pretreatment assessment, surveillance, or evaluation for suspected recurrence. MRI pelvis without and with intravenous contrast is usually appropriate for assessment of local tumor extension across histologic subtypes and grades. For aggressive histologic tumor types, or when metastatic disease is suspected, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for evaluation of nodal and distant metastases. Routine imaging surveillance is usually not appropriate for asymptomatic patients with treated low- or intermediate-risk disease, whereas CT may be appropriate in selected asymptomatic high-risk patients. MRI pelvis, CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and FDG-PET/CT are usually appropriate for suspected recurrence. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.
authors: Expert Panel on GYN and OB Imaging

articles.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Staging and Follow-Up of Biliary Cancer.
articles.abstract: Biliary tract cancers, comprising gallbladder cancer and intrahepatic and extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, are uncommon but aggressive malignancies that are often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Accurate staging is critical because patients with localized disease may be candidates for curative resection, whereas those with unresectable or metastatic disease are triaged to systemic and palliative therapy. This document reviews the evidence for imaging in five clinical scenarios: locoregional staging of gallbladder cancer, locoregional staging of cholangiocarcinoma, staging of distant metastatic disease, posttreatment evaluation, and surveillance. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the abdomen are the mainstays of locoregional assessment, whereas CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and FDG-PET are used for distant staging and follow-up. The American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria are evidence-based guidelines for specific clinical conditions that are reviewed annually by a multidisciplinary expert panel. The guideline development and revision process support the systematic analysis of the medical literature from peer reviewed journals. Established methodology principles such as Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation or GRADE are adapted to evaluate the evidence. The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method User Manual provides the methodology to determine the appropriateness of imaging and treatment procedures for specific clinical scenarios. In those instances where peer reviewed literature is lacking or equivocal, experts may be the primary evidentiary source available to formulate a recommendation.

articles.title: Vascular Abnormalities in the Hand and Wrist: State-of-the-Art Multimodality Imaging.
articles.abstract: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.

articles.title: Predicting Prognosis in Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis: Conventional to Functional MRI.
articles.abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic fibroinflammatory cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal biliary strictures, cholestasis, and an increased risk of hepatobiliary malignancy and liver failure. MRI and MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) are central to diagnosis, surveillance, and risk stratification. Recent consensus guidelines from the International PSC Study Group emphasize standardized reporting for PSC with MRI and MRCP. Beyond anatomic assessment, established and emerging quantitative and functional imaging biomarkers include liver stiffness measurements, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction, and relative hepatobiliary phase enhancement. Imaging-based scoring systems such as Assessment of Noncontrast MRI for Advanced Liver Imaging (ANALI) scores provide additional prognostic information and correlate with clinical outcomes and established risk models. Hepatocyte-specific contrast-enhanced MRI allows evaluation of biliary excretion and regional liver function, facilitating identification of functional strictures and parenchymal dysfunction. The authors review current MRI and MRCP reporting standards, prognostic scoring systems, and evolving functional MRI techniques, with an emphasis on practical implementation in clinical radiology practice. ©RSNA, 2026 See the invited commentary by Ba-Ssalamah in this issue.

articles.title: Imaging and Complications of Meckel Diverticulum.
articles.abstract: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, yet it is frequently asymptomatic. Meckel diverticulum poses unique diagnostic challenges due to its variable manifestation and infrequent visualization at imaging. The authors review the embryology and anatomy of Meckel diverticulum, its normal radiologic appearances, and its complications and their management. Complications of Meckel diverticulum occur in up to 4%-9% of patients. Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is more common in children but can also be seen in adults. A giant Meckel diverticulum, presence of ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, or adjacent adhesions and bands are associated with a higher likelihood of a symptomatic manifestation. The most common complications include small-bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, and diverticulitis. Children more commonly present with gastrointestinal bleeding, while diverticulitis is more common in adults. Small-bowel obstruction can occur at any age and can be secondary to inversion of Meckel diverticulum, intussusception, volvulus, internal or external hernias, neoplasms, enteroliths, congenital bands, or postinflammatory changes. When a patient presents with acute abdomen or gastrointestinal bleeding, the choice of imaging modalities includes CT or US, with the latter preferred in the pediatric population. Technetium 99m-pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan) can be additionally performed to evaluate rectal bleeding in younger patients. MRI is reserved as a problem-solving tool. Meckel diverticulum should be differentiated from its common imaging mimics (eg, the appendix, ileal duplication cyst, and mesenteric small-bowel diverticulum). When Meckel diverticulum is not visualized at imaging, the radiologist still plays a key role by raising suspicion for an underlying Meckel diverticulum and identifying other critical imaging findings that can inform clinical management. An understanding of the common clinical manifestations associated with Meckel diverticulum and a systematic imaging approach can improve preoperative diagnosis and patient management.

articles.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests. RESULTS: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). CONCLUSION: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Patterns of Progression on Posttreatment Imaging During [177Lu]Lu-PSMA Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
articles.abstract: We characterized patterns of treatment response and progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) using serial posttreatment SPECT/CT and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET imaging and evaluated cycle-by-cycle prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-imaging concordance. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 361 patients from 2 academic centers who received at least 2 cycles of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT between May 2017 and March 2025. Posttreatment SPECT/CT scans were qualitatively evaluated to determine the site and pattern of response and progression, including PSMA low-avidity and PSMA-negative disease. Progression was defined by the appearance of new lesions or at least a 2-fold growth in preexisting lesions on SPECT/CT. PSA response was defined per Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 criteria as at least a 50% decline from baseline. For cycle-by-cycle concordance analysis, PSA change was classified directionally as rising or falling relative to the prior cycle. In patients who paused or completed RPT after response, progression imaging was compared with the final on-treatment SPECT/CT scan. Results: Overall, 290 of 361 (80%) patients demonstrated a decrease in lesion size or number on posttreatment imaging. Of 312 patients with baseline bone disease, 81% demonstrated a response on posttreatment imaging. In total, 156 of 361 patients (43%) demonstrated progression during treatment. New osseous lesions developed in 132 patients, of whom 89 (67%) had PSMA low-avidity disease. At cycle 2, 64% of new lesions were osseous, increasing to at least 90% by cycles 4-6. PSMA-negative progression occurred in 22 patients (6%), predominantly in the liver (n = 11) and lymph nodes (n = 8), with 59% detected at cycle 2. Among 81 patients with imaging available at PSA progression after treatment completion or pause, 74 (91%) had imaging progression; of these, 69 (93%) demonstrated osseous and 13 (18%) nodal progression. PSA and imaging were discordant in 25%-43% of patients across cycles, with discordance increasing from cycle 2 to cycle 6. Conclusion: Progression during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT occurs most frequently in bone, with 67% of patients with new osseous lesions demonstrating a PSMA low-avidity disease component. PSMA-negative progression is uncommon and tends to emerge early. PSA-imaging discordance is frequent, underscoring the need for integrated imaging assessment throughout treatment.

articles.title: Impact of PSMA PET/CT Staging on Long-Term Outcomes in Patients with Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: Results of a Large Single-Center Cohort.
articles.abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT has become the gold standard for staging and restaging prostate cancer, with superior diagnostic accuracy over conventional imaging and established prognostic value. However, there are limited data on whether PSMA PET/CT-improved staging accuracy is associated with improved long-term patient outcomes. This study analyzes the association between PSMA PET/CT at primary staging and overall survival (OS), biochemical recurrence (BCR), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) in a large university hospital cohort at a center where PSMA PET/CT has been clinically available for over 13 y. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included all 11,146 patients with prostate cancer diagnosed between 2013 and 2023. The final analysis cohort consisted of 6999 patients, of whom 505 (7.2%) underwent PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. We classified patients into 3 groups using D'Amico risk classification. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier methods and adjusted Cox regression models. To control for selection bias, propensity score matching and overlap weighting were applied. Landmark analysis addressed selection and immortal time biases, and Fine-Gray models accounted for competing risk of death in a BCR analysis. Results: PSMA PET/CT was associated with a longer time to BCR (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38-0.68; P < 0.001), longer CSS (HR = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.61; P < 0.001), and longer OS (HR = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; P < 0.001). PSMA PET imaging was associated with particularly better outcomes in high-risk patients, especially those treated with radiotherapy. In the radiotherapy group, the HRs were 0.42 for OS, 0.42 for BCR, and 0.25 for CSS (all P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed in patients undergoing radical prostatectomy. As the formal interaction test between PSMA PET/CT and treatment modality was not statistically significant, this differential finding should be considered exploratory. Across all 9 sensitivity analyses, HRs were consistently below 1, indicating a uniform direction of benefit. Conclusion: The association observed in this large real-world cohort supports the clinical value of PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. Findings were particularly favorable among high-risk patients undergoing radiotherapy, although this subgroup difference should be interpreted as exploratory given the nonsignificant interaction test. These results support a potential role for PSMA PET/CT in improving patient selection and detecting oligometastatic disease, enabling higher precision in treatment planning.

articles.title: Role of [18F]F-Fluciclovine PET/CT in Patients with Biochemical Recurrence of Prostate Cancer and Negative PSMA PET Results: A Single-Center Study.
articles.abstract: Our purpose was to evaluate whether [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT detects sites of disease in patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR) of prostate cancer and negative findings on prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET and to assess its impact on intended management. Methods: In this prospective single-arm study (NCT05722925), 50 patients with BCR (prostate-specific antigen [PSA] ≥ 0.2 ng/mL) and negative findings on PSMA PET underwent [18F]F-fluciclovine PET/CT within 30 d of the previous imaging. Detection rate, distribution of disease, PSA-stratified analysis, management impact, and correct localization rate were assessed using descriptive statistics and exact CI. Results: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET had positive findings in 28 of 50 patients (56%; 95% CI, 41%-70%). Disease was confined to the prostate bed in 14 patients (50%), whereas 14 (50%) demonstrated nodal or distant metastases. Detection rate increased with PSA, from 44% at a PSA of 0.2-0.5 ng/mL to 100% at a PSA of 5 ng/mL or higher. The intended management changed in 71% of patients after the [18F]F-fluciclovine PET: 87% of patients with positive findings and 54% with negative findings. Among patients with an available reference standard (n = 14), all positive findings were confirmed to be true-positive. Conclusion: [18F]F-fluciclovine PET detected recurrent disease in over half of patients with negative PSMA PET findings and frequently altered management, supporting its complementary role in selected patients with BCR.

articles.title: 18F-BMS-986192 PET to Predict Durable Response to Nivolumab in NSCLC: A Novel Approach Beyond PD-L1 Immunohistochemistry.
articles.abstract: Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry, the current standard biomarker for predicting response to programmed death protein 1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer, has moderate predictive value among others because of tumor heterogeneity and limited biopsy representation, whereas PD-L1 PET/CT using 18F-BMS-986192 enables noninvasive, whole-tumor assessment of PD-L1 expression and heterogeneity, potentially improving prediction of response to immunotherapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter biomarker exploration study, patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer eligible for nivolumab-based therapies underwent baseline 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT, 18F-FDG PET/CT, and tumor biopsy for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry before treatment initiation. The primary endpoint was durable clinical benefit, defined as progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 mo or greater, with secondary analyses assessing associations among tracer uptake, PD-L1 expression, survival outcomes, and PET-based radiomic features. Results: Of 91 enrolled patients, 77 were included in the final analysis of 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT. Although PD-L1 immunohistochemistry did not differ between patients with PFS of less than 9 mo versus 9 mo or greater, PD-L1 PET uptake in lung lesions was significantly higher in patients with PFS of at least 9 mo (P = 0.01). Using an optimal mean SUVpeak cutoff of 2.4, PD-L1 PET demonstrated a high negative predictive value (94%) for durable clinical benefit, with significant associations for both PFS and overall survival, particularly in patients receiving first-line treatment. Tracer uptake showed no correlation with 18F-FDG uptake. Conclusion: 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT revealed interpatient PD-L1 variability. Low uptake in lung lesions predicted poor outcomes with high negative predictive value. 18F-BMS-986192 PET/CT demonstrated stronger negative predictive value than did baseline PD-L1 immunohistochemistry in this cohort. These findings require prospective validation.

articles.title: Botulinum Toxin Plus Transdermal Scopolamine Reduces Salivary Gland Uptake in Patients Undergoing Tandem Radiopharmaceutical Therapy with [225Ac]Ac- and [177Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligands.
articles.abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has shown remarkable efficacy in advanced metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. However, salivary gland toxicity is a major dose-limiting adverse effect, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides such as 225Ac. Although tandem therapy with combined [225Ac]Ac- and [177Lu]Lu-labeled PSMA-targeted RPT in a single low-activity cycle may address certain challenges, effective salivary gland protection remains crucial. In this study, we explored the use of botulinum toxin (BTX) type A (incobotulinumtoxinA) plus transdermal scopolamine as a protective strategy to mitigate salivary gland uptake of PSMA radioligands. Methods: IncobotulinumtoxinA was injected percutaneously, with increasing dosages of up to 300 units distributed into the parotid and submandibular glands under ultrasound guidance, a mean of 24 d before scheduled tandem PSMA RPT. Transdermal scopolamine was applied from 72 h before RPT until 2 h after RPT. Molecular imaging was conducted as per PSMA RPT protocol, with pretreatment PSMA PET/CT to confirm ligand uptake and follow-up PET/CT for restaging. SPECT/CT was conducted as imaging after RPT. PET SUVmean or SPECT counts were measured, and ratios of injected-to-noninjected contralateral glands were calculated and compared before and after BTX. Results: Fourteen patients (mean age, 68.0 ± 8.1 y) were included; 1 patient received 2 injections before his treatment, and another underwent 2 tandem RPT cycles, with BTX administered before each cycle. Mean cumulative administered activity was 5.05 ± 1.09 GBq for 177Lu and 6.87 ± 3.14 MBq for 225Ac. Combination therapy with incobotulinumtoxinA plus transdermal scopolamine was associated with lower PSMA radioligand uptake in BTX-treated salivary glands relative to untreated contralateral glands, with mean reductions of approximately 30% in parotid glands and 17% in submandibular glands compared with untreated glands. Up to 300 units of incobotulinumtoxinA distributed among the major salivary glands was safe. No patient discontinued tandem PSMA therapy because of xerostomia, and no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were observed during PSMA RPT. Conclusion: BTX plus transdermal scopolamine is a promising strategy to reduce salivary gland uptake during PSMA RPT. This approach enhances patient quality of life after PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy, particularly with α-emitting radionuclides, while preserving its excellent therapeutic efficacy.

articles.title: Predicting [90Y]Y-FAPI-46 Tumor Absorbed Dose from Single-Time-Point [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT Imaging.
articles.abstract: Radiolabeled fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeting peptides, such as 90Y-FAPI-46, have increasingly been used to treat various tumor entities, with preliminary reports indicating therapeutic responses with acceptable toxicity profiles. Dosimetry can be used to maximize antitumor capability and minimize side effects. The aim of this study was to investigate whether 90Y-FAPI-46 tumor dosimetry can be predicted by diagnostic 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT data. Methods: Fourteen patients with 24 lesions underwent a single-time-point 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT scan and 3 90Y-FAPI-46 PET/CT scans for dosimetry within a 3-mo interval. Tumors were identified on PET images, and the anatomic tumor volume was measured on low-dose CT. Tumor uptake extrapolated at time of injection, time-integrated activity coefficient (TIAC), and tumor absorbed dose were calculated as reference values using 90Y-FAPI-46 data and compared with the corresponding predicted values using 68Ga-FAPI-46 data by means of a single-time-point dosimetry model. Correlations between 90Y-FAPI-46- and 68Ga-FAPI-46-based values were assessed. Results: In calculating the predicted values using a single-time-point 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT, the mean effective half-life of 90Y-FAPI-46 across all lesions was 8.44 ± 1.73 h. The mean ± SD ratio (i.e., the predicted values using 68Ga-FAPI-46 data divided by the reference 90Y-FAPI-46 data) were 0.93 ± 0.39, 0.77 ± 0.35, and 0.77 ± 0.35 for tumor uptake, TIAC, and tumor absorbed dose, respectively. In the Bland-Altman analysis, mean differences (bias) ± SD of the percent differences of tumor uptake, TIAC, and tumor absorbed dose were -16.11% ± 43.28% (95% CI, -100.90 to 68.73%; Spearman ρ = 0.91; P < 0.0001), -32.60% ± 41.26% (95% CI, -113.50 to 48.26%; Spearman ρ = 0.91; P < 0.0001), and -33.35% ± 40.19% (95% CI, -112.10 to 45.43%; Spearman ρ = 0.77; P < 0.0001), respectively. Conclusion: Tumor uptake, TIAC, and tumor absorbed dose on 90Y-FAPI-46 PET/CT and 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT were highly correlated, although the values on 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT tended to be lower than those on 90Y-FAPI-46 PET/CT. Predicted values on 68Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT can help clinicians with diagnostic stratification and patient selection, with intratherapeutic verification remaining necessary before any individualization of administered activity.

articles.title: Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen PET/CT Complements MRI for Focal Therapy Selection in Prostate Cancer: A Whole-Mount Histopathologic Study.
articles.abstract: The incremental value of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT over multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for selecting patients for prostate cancer focal therapy is undefined. Unlike lesion-detection studies, we evaluated whether PSMA PET/CT, mpMRI, and their combination correctly determine focal therapy eligibility when validated against whole-mount histopathology (WMHP). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP) at UCLA (2017-2024) with preoperative PSMA PET/CT and mpMRI, a biopsy grade group (GG) of 3 or less, unilateral disease, and a prostate-specific antigen level of less than 20 ng/mL. Two blinded readers per modality assessed extraprostatic extension (EPE), seminal vesicle invasion (SVI), bilateral disease, and multifocality; a third adjudicated discordances. Eligibility required the absence of all 4. On WMHP, ineligibility was EPE, SVI, multifocal or bilateral disease with a contralateral or secondary GG of at least 2 nodules, or any GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Modalities were compared by McNemar tests. Results: Of 112 patients, 77 (69%) were ineligible on WMHP, including 19 (17%) with a GG greater than 3 focus at RP. Sensitivity and specificity were 53% and 54% for PET and 70% and 49% for mpMRI. Combined imaging improved sensitivity to 83% (P < 0.001 vs. PET; P = 0.002 vs. MRI) but reduced specificity to 26%. Per 100 patients at this prevalence, this would correctly identify approximately 9 additional ineligible patients while falsely excluding approximately 7 true candidates. mpMRI was more sensitive than PET for EPE (77% vs. 32%, P < 0.001), whereas PET was more specific (90% vs. 58%, P < 0.001). Combined imaging improved detection of multifocal (44% vs. 23%, P = 0.001) and bilateral disease (45% vs. 23%, P = 0.002) versus MRI alone. Conclusion: Adding PSMA PET/CT to mpMRI significantly improves sensitivity for exclusionary features, reflecting complementary molecular and anatomic information. However, combined imaging still misses a substantial proportion of adverse pathology, so imaging alone should not determine eligibility.

articles.title: Symptomatic Hyperkinetic Gallbladder: An Unrecognized Indication for Cholecystectomy.
articles.abstract: For decades, low gallbladder ejection fraction (GBEF), measured with hepatobiliary scintigraphy after infusion of sincalide, has been used to diagnose symptomatic biliary hypokinesia and as a predictor of the necessity for cholecystectomy. Recently, gallbladder hypercontractility (GBEF > 79%) has been recognized as a cause of right upper quadrant pain, and cholecystectomy has often resulted in symptom relief. This retrospective study evaluated follow-up data collected after GBEF studies to determine the incidence of cholecystectomy or persistence of symptoms. Methods: We evaluated all GBEF biliary studies performed at our institution between January 1, 2012, and December 31, 2025. Study reports containing "ejection fraction" and "sincalide" were identified to establish the study population. All patients presented with right upper quadrant pain. They received 185 MBq (range, 111-259 MBq) of 99mTc-mebrofenin intravenously and were imaged in a 20° left anterior oblique position for 60 min. Once the gallbladder was clearly seen, the patients were given a 30-min intravenous infusion of sincalide (0.02 μg/kg), and imaging was continued for a total of 45 min. Patients were categorized as having probable gallbladder disease (cholecystectomy and resolution of symptoms or no cholecystectomy and persistent symptoms) or unlikely gallbladder disease (cholecystectomy and persistent symptoms or no cholecystectomy and resolved symptoms or other diagnosis). Results: In total, 1775 patients were included in the final analysis. Forty percent of patients had a GBEF of greater than 79%, and 27% had a GBEF of less than 39%. Of those who underwent cholecystectomy, 90% of those with a GBEF of less than 39% and 94% of those with a GBEF of greater than 79% experienced symptom relief. The incidence of probable biliary disease was 61% in patients with a low GBEF and 44% in patients with a high GBEF and was lowest in the group with a GBEF of 60%-69% (24% of patients). Conclusion: Our study found that hepatobiliary GBEF is not as accurate as we have assumed. Additional clinical criteria are needed to improve patient selection and positive outcomes. The high percentage of patients with a GBEF exceeding 79% has not been appreciated, as most of the previous studies evaluated healthy subjects and did not examine outcomes. These results should shift how we think about GBEF studies and how the results are reported.

articles.title: Adoption of ACR TI-RADS and Documentation of Biopsy Criteria in Thyroid Ultrasound Reports: A Seven-Year Analysis of a National Radiology Network.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate longitudinal adoption of American College of Radiology (ACR) Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) Terminology, report-level documentation of Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) criteria, and associated ultrasound-guided FNA practice in a large multisite radiology network. METHODS: In this retrospective, multicenter study across 89 imaging sites, 304,455 diagnostic thyroid ultrasound reports (CPT 76536) and 11,246 ultrasound-guided FNA reports (CPT 10005/10006) from 2017 through 2023 were analyzed. A linked pre-biopsy cohort of 994 diagnostic reports immediately preceding FNA was examined. Automated text mining identified TI-RADS language and documentation of nodules meeting ACR size-based FNA thresholds. Trends were assessed using Cochran-Armitage, Spearman correlation, and χ2 tests. RESULTS: TI-RADS language increased from 1.6% of thyroid ultrasound reports in 2017 to 54.1% in 2023. Among 112,036 TI-RADS-containing reports, 11,845 (10.6%) documented nodules meeting FNA criteria. This proportion declined from 23.3% in 2017 to 8.0% in 2023, an absolute decline of 15.3 percentage points (Z = -47.94, P < 0.001) and was inversely correlated with annual TI-RADS adoption across the seven annual observations (ρ = -1.000, P < 0.001). Among FNA-indicated reports, TR4 predominated (56.9%), followed by TR3 (21.0%) and TR5 (19.4%); category distribution shifted significantly over time, although the effect size was small (χ2 = 169.91, P < 0.001; Cramér's V=0.086). In the pre-biopsy cohort (n=994), 498 (50.1%) contained TI-RADS language. The FNA rate per 1,000 thyroid ultrasound examination remained stable (29.1 in 2017; 27.7 in 2023). CONCLUSION: ACR TI-RADS terminology use increased substantially but remained incomplete. Increasing terminology use was associated with declining report-level FNA eligibility. Biopsy appropriateness could not be assessed from report-level documentation alone.

articles.title: "Where the Money Goes: Institutional Distribution of NIH Funding Among Radiology Clinician-Scientists (2012-2025)".
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prior analyses of National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding to radiology departments have characterized aggregate grant volume and funding levels but have not systematically examined the institutional landscape of clinician-led research. This study characterized the institutional distribution of NIH funding awarded to clinician principal investigators (PIs) in diagnostic radiology (DR), interventional radiology (IR), and radiation oncology (RO) from fiscal years 2012 through 2025. METHODS: In this retrospective cross-sectional analysis, grant records were extracted from the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools Expenditures and Results (RePORTER) database and filtered to PIs with an institutional department designation of "Radiation-Diagnostic/Oncology." Clinician investigators were identified by cross-referencing with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) datasets. Institutional funding, grant counts, unique investigators, grant mechanism portfolios, and career development awards were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 437 unique clinician investigators (DR: 226; IR: 46; RO: 165) were identified, accounting for $1.65 billion in inflation-adjusted funding. NIH-funded clinicians were distributed across 47 institutions in DR, 29 in IR, and 45 in RO. The top five institutions accounted for 34.5% of grants and 38.4% of total funding, largely reflecting workforce size: institutional clinician PI count explained 82% of the variance in funding, and funding per clinician PI was more evenly distributed (Gini 0.38) than total funding (Gini 0.62). Stanford received the largest grant funding in DR ($134.9M), UC San Francisco in IR ($36.9M), and University of Michigan in RO ($68.1M). R01 awards were the dominant mechanism across all subspecialties. Forty new K-awards were issued across 21 institutions. CONCLUSIONS: NIH funding to radiology clinician investigators is concentrated at a small number of academic medical centers, principally because those centers host larger clinician investigator workforces, with a narrow clinician-scientist pipeline. These findings identify opportunities to broaden research capacity across the radiology workforce.

articles.title: Learning discriminative prototypes via Variational Information Bottleneck for multimodal cancer survival prediction.
articles.abstract: Survival prediction is critical in cancer research for forecasting patient outcomes and optimizing treatment strategies. While integrating histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) with genomic profiles holds promise for improved predictive accuracy, two major challenges persist: (1) the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio in gigapixel WSIs, where task-irrelevant background patches often dominate standard Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) bags, and (2) the instability of unsupervised prototype initialization (e.g., K-means), which frequently converges to non-informative morphological patterns. To address these challenges, we propose DP-VIB (Discriminative Prototypes via Variational Information Bottleneck), a hierarchical framework that leverages the information bottleneck principle to learn survival-relevant prototypes in a coarse-to-fine manner. Unlike traditional approaches, DP-VIB first employs a survival-supervised Global VIB Module to learn a discriminative latent representation, filtering out nuisance variations through an information bottleneck constraint. Subsequently, Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) priors derived from this purified latent representation serve as robust initializations for fine-grained patch-level prototypes, significantly enhancing convergence and semantic quality. Finally, we introduce a tri-branch Histology-Genomics(HG) encoder followed by a cross-modal fusion mechanism to deeply fuse these VIB-guided prototypes with genomic pathway embeddings, enabling analysis of model-derived prototype-pathway associations. Extensive validation on five TCGA cancer cohorts demonstrates that DP-VIB consistently outperforms strong baselines in Concordance Index (C-index), achieving superior robustness and accuracy in individualized survival prediction.

articles.title: Invited Commentary: Beyond Morphology: Toward a Multiparametric MRI Score for Precision Risk Stratification in Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis.
GeoMind: Dancing with Geometric Brain Rhythm on Symmetric Positive Definite Manifolds.
articles.abstract: State space model (SSM) is a powerful tool in neuroscience field to characterize the dynamic nature of brain functions by elucidating the mechanism of how brain system transits between brain states and how underlying states give rise to the observed neural activities. Although tremendous efforts have been made to lend the power of deep learning and mathematical insight of SSM in various functional neuroimaging studies, current state-of-the-art methods lack a holistic view of brain state evolution as a self-organized dynamical system where each part of the brain is functionally inter-connected. Since the topological co-activation of functional fluctuations exhibits an intrinsic geometric pattern (symmetric and positive definite, SPD) on the Riemannian manifold, the call for understanding how a selective set of functional connectivities in the brain supports diverse behavior and cognition emerge a new machine learning scenario of manifold-based SSM for largescale functional neuroimages. To that end, we propose a geometric neural network of SSM, coined GeoMind, designed to uncover evolving brain states by tracking the trajectory of functional dynamics on a high-dimensional Riemannian manifold of SPD matrices. GeoMind demonstrates promising results in identifying specific brain states on task-based functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, as well as in diseases early diagnosis for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and Autism, by using resting-state fMRI. These results highlight the applicability of GeoMind in neuroscience research. To further evaluate generalizability of GeoMind, we applied GeoMind to electroencephalography (EEG) emotion datasets, outperforming competing methods and demonstrating scalability across neuroimaging modalities.

articles.title: DuMeta++: Spatiotemporal Dual Meta-Learning for Generalizable Few-Shot Brain Tissue Segmentation Across Diverse Ages.
articles.abstract: Accurate segmentation of brain tissues from MRI scans is critical for neuroscience and clinical applications, but achieving consistent performance across the human lifespan remains challenging due to dynamic, age-related changes in brain appearance and morphology. While prior work has sought to mitigate these shifts by using self-supervised regularization with paired longitudinal data, such data are often unavailable in practice. To address this, we propose DuMeta++, a dual meta-learning framework that operates without paired longitudinal data. Our approach integrates: (1) meta-feature learning to extract age-agnostic semantic representations of spatiotemporally evolving brain structures, and (2) meta-initialization learning to enable data-efficient adaptation of the segmentation model. Furthermore, we propose a memory-bank-based class-aware regularization strategy to enforce longitudinal consistency without explicit longitudinal super-vision. We further characterize the convergence of the dual meta-learning pipeline under standard smoothness assumptions. Extensive experiments on the iSeg-2019 and ADNI datasets under one- and five-shot settings demonstrate that DuMeta++ consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both segmentation accuracy and longitudinal consistency. Code will be available at https:// github.com/ladderlab-xjtu/DuMeta++.

The role of artificial intelligence in predicting late-onset intrauterine growth restriction in singleton pregnancies: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Late-onset intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is difficult to detect and is associated with adverse perinatal outcomes. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning (ML) and deep learning, for predicting late-onset IUGR in singleton pregnancies. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published during the past decade that used AI to predict IUGR. Nineteen studies including 13,379 pregnancies were analyzed. Sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and diagnostic odds ratios were pooled using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models; the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was estimated in STATA. RESULTS: In the primary analysis (one model per study, k=17), pooled sensitivity was 0.83 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89), specificity was 0.89 (95% CI, 0.85 to 0.91), the positive and negative likelihood ratios were 6.6 (95% CI, 5.3 to 8.1) and 0.22 (95% CI, 0.16 to 0.30), and the AUC was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.91 to 0.95). Estimates were unchanged when all model entries were included (k=51). No threshold effect or funnel-plot asymmetry was detected. Subgroup estimates for support vector machines, random forests, and logistic regression were similar but reflected indirect comparisons. CONCLUSION: AI/ML models showed high pooled discriminative accuracy for late-onset IUGR. However, the evidence derives mainly from retrospective, single-center case-control studies without external validation; calibration was reported in six of 19 studies and decision-curve analysis in none. These estimates are an optimistic upper bound, not evidence of superiority over current ultrasound practice.

FDG PET/MR for liver metastases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy and technical protocols with a proposed reporting framework.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic performance of FDG PET/MR for detecting hepatic metastases from extrahepatic primary malignancies, together with acquisition protocols, reconstruction parameters, and technical heterogeneity. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted through September 2026. Eligible studies evaluated FDG PET/MR for hepatic metastases and reported diagnostic performance data and/or technical protocol information. Summary estimates of sensitivity and specificity were obtained using a bivariate random-effects model. A structured qualitative assessment of PET and MR acquisition, reconstruction parameters, and image interpretation strategies was also performed. RESULTS: Fifteen studies involving 861 patients met the inclusion criteria. Eight studies (53%) provided sufficient data for the diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis, whereas all contributed to the qualitative technical assessment. The meta-analysis demonstrated a summary sensitivity estimate of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89-0.97) and a summary specificity estimate of 0.99 (95% CI, 0.92-1.00) for detecting hepatic metastases. Sensitivity showed substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.83), whereas specificity showed low heterogeneity (I² = 0.21). Technical assessment revealed marked variability in PET acquisition, MR protocols, reconstruction parameters, and reporting, with frequent underreporting of voxel size, filtering, and motion correction. Hepatobiliary contrast agents were used in only a minority of studies, and dedicated PET motion correction was rarely implemented. CONCLUSION: FDG PET/MR demonstrates high lesion-level diagnostic accuracy for the detection of hepatic metastases, with high summary sensitivity and specificity. However, substantial between-study variability in sensitivity, together with variability and frequent underreporting of technical parameters, highlights the need for standardized acquisition protocols and reporting frameworks to improve reproducibility, comparability, and clinical translation.

articles.title: Improved Upper-Airway Collapse Imaging in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Self-Supervised Spiral Variational Manifold Learning.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To propose a self-supervised variational manifold learning framework for dynamic upper-airway MRI reconstruction in obstructive sleep apnea from prospectively under-sampled spiral data during natural sleep, without requiring fully sampled training data. METHODS: A CNN generator and low-dimensional latent vectors were jointly optimized directly from prospectively under-sampled spiral k-space measurements, learning a subject-specific temporal manifold without an explicit motion model. A validation loss guided adaptive learning rate provided principled early stopping without ground truth. Eleven concurrent axial slices from velo-pharynx to hypo-pharynx were reconstructed at 183 ms temporal resolution and 11 ×  acceleration across 8 OSA patients during natural sleep and 4 healthy volunteers performing the Müller maneuver. Reconstruction quality was compared against parallel imaging, compressed sensing, view sharing, and analysis-manifold reconstruction. Three expert raters independently assessed image quality using a four-point ordinal rubric. RESULTS: The proposed method resolved multi-site airway collapse across 11 contiguous slices, including simultaneous visualization of complete concentric retro-palatal collapse, lateral collapse at the velo-pharyngeal to oro-pharyngeal transition, and partial tongue-base and oropharyngeal narrowing. Expert scores were superior across aliasing, spatial blurring, and temporal blurring categories ( p < 0.001  , pairwise Mann-Whitney U tests). Reconstructed airway dynamics were corroborated by concurrent respiratory effort and SpO   2   signals, with up to 13 obstructive events identified within a single imaging run. Reconstruction artifacts occurred in 8 of 132 slices (6%) and did not compromise airway visualization. CONCLUSION: Self-supervised variational manifold learning demonstrates the feasibility of robust dynamic upper-airway MRI during natural sleep, with potential to inform future OSA phenotyping and surgical-planning studies.

articles.title: Population-Specific CT-Derived Sarcopenia Cutoff Values and Inter-Vertebral Level Correlations in Healthy Thai Adults Using Automated Muscle Segmentation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Establishing optimal sarcopenia cutoffs is essential, as L3 is not always included in CT imaging, and reference levels vary across populations. The absence of Southeast Asia-specific thresholds may lead to misclassification, highlighting the need for regionally appropriate diagnostic criteria. This study establishes population-specific sarcopenia cutoffs (T10-S1) in the Thai population and defines BMI-adjusted thresholds. It also assesses skeletal muscle index correlations across vertebral levels to refine L3-based sarcopenia evaluation. METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed 475 healthy Thai adults (aged 18-40 years) who underwent emergency department CT between January 2010 and June 2023. Skeletal muscle parameters were measured from T10 to S1 using custom software. Measurements included skeletal muscle area (SMA), skeletal muscle radiation attenuation (SMRA), skeletal muscle index (SMI), and height-adjusted skeletal muscle index (SMIH1). Sex-stratified analyses and correlations between vertebral levels were performed. RESULTS: At L3, sarcopenia cutoffs using SMI and SMIH1 were 23.3 cm²/m² and 37.1 cm²/m for females, and 31.3 cm²/m² and 53.9 cm²/m for males, respectively. Strong correlations were observed between L3 and adjacent vertebral levels (r > 0.8), with correlation strength decreasing with anatomical distance. Application of international cutoffs to the Thai population resulted in overestimation of sarcopenia cases. BMI-adjusted variable thresholds demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy compared to fixed cutoffs. CONCLUSION: This study establishes the first population-specific sarcopenia reference values for Thai adults and validates the use of alternative vertebral levels when L3 imaging is unavailable. Our findings emphasize the importance of population-specific and BMI-adjusted cutoff values for accurate sarcopenia diagnosis in Thai adults. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This study establishes the first population-specific sarcopenia cutoff values for healthy Thai adults, providing the first evidence-based reference standards for the Thai populations. At L3, the recommended cutoffs are SMI 23.3 cm²/m² and SMIH1 37.1 cm²/m for females, and SMI 31.3 cm²/m² and SMIH1 53.9 cm²/m for males. Strong correlations (r > 0.8) between L3 and adjacent vertebral levels validate the use of alternative assessment sites when L3 imaging is unavailable: T12-L1 for chest CT protocols, L3 for abdominal CT protocols, and L4-L5 for pelvic CT protocols. Application of Western cutoffs to the Thai populations results in significant overestimation of sarcopenia prevalence, emphasizing the critical importance of population-specific diagnostic criteria.

articles.title: Thermal Ablation versus Surgical Resection for US-Detected Solitary cT1N0M0 Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma in Elderly Patients: A Multicenter Comparative Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study was aimed to compare the effectiveness and complication rates of thermal ablation (TA) versus surgical resection (SR) in managing US-Detected solitary T1N0M0 papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in elderly patients, including those with occult lymph node metastasis (LNM). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter study involved 225 elderly patients with solitary PTC who underwent TA or SR. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to minimize confounding factors. After PSM, the SR group was divided into SR-T1N0 and SR-T1N1 subgroups based on postoperative lymph node pathology. Disease progression and complications were compared across groups. RESULTS: Seventy-eight patients underwent TA, and 147 underwent SR. No significant difference in disease progression was found (2.6% vs. 1.4%; p = 0.860), including new tumors and LNM. After PSM, no differences were observed between groups (TA vs. SR-T1N0/SR-T1N1) (p > 0.05). Major complications were similar, but permanent hoarseness and hypoparathyroidism occurred only in the SR group. The TA group had significantly fewer side effects (0% vs. 25.9%, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: In elderly patients with US-detected solitary T1N0M0 PTC, disease progression was similar between TA and SR. However, TA better preserves thyroid function, making it a safer and effective treatment for this population. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This study demonstrates that TA is as effective as SR in elderly patients with US-detected solitary T1N0M0 PTC, including those with occult LNM, while better preserving organ function. This makes it a viable option for patients unable or unwilling to undergo SR.

articles.title: MRI-based proton density fat fraction combined with adipose tissue for identifying metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop a non-invasive diagnostic model combining magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived proton density fat fraction (PDFF) and adipose tissue for identifying metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 197 consecutive patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) who underwent liver biopsy, MRI-PDFF, and transient elastography (TE) were retrospectively enrolled. Independent predictors of MASH were identified using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses. A combined model was constructed and internally validated via 1000 bootstrap resamples. The diagnostic performance was compared with that of established non-invasive tests (NITs). RESULTS: Multivariable logistic regression analyses demonstrated that the PDFF and total adipose tissue index (TATI) were independent risk factors for MASH. The MRI-based PDFF-adipose tissue (MR-PAT) model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.866 for MASH identification. Bootstrap internal validation yielded an AUC of 0.870. The performance of the models was consistent across clinically relevant subgroups. The diagnostic performance of the MR-PAT model for MASH identification was significantly better than that of all the established NITs (all p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: The MR-PAT model, combining MRI-derived PDFF and TATI, provides an accurate and robust non-invasive tool for identifying MASH. It outperforms widely recognized NITs and holds promise for risk stratification in patients with MASLD. KEY POINTS: Question MASH is a critical histological endpoint of MASLD, but reliable non-invasive tools for its assessment remain inadequate. Findings The MR-PAT model integrating MRI-based PDFF and adipose tissue quantification demonstrates robust and excellent diagnostic performance for identifying MASH. Critical Relevance Statement The MR-PAT model leverages hepatic steatosis and the adipose tissue burden to elucidate the pathophysiological mechanisms driving steatohepatitis. It can serve as an accurate, non-invasive tool for identifying MASH and holds promise for risk stratification in patients with MASLD.

articles.title: A semi-supervised diffusion model for automated segmentation of vascular plaques.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Segmenting vascular plaques in the carotid arteries, aorta, and iliac arteries on CT is important because plaque burden relates to cardiovascular and stroke risk and can guide treatment. However, manual labeling is often infeasible and time-consuming across large vascular regions. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) can leverage unlabeled CT data to enable accurate plaque segmentation with only limited labels. METHODS: We applied a diffusion-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) method for vascular plaque segmentation in non-contrast CT by formulating the task as multi-class segmentation of plaques and 26 adjacent anatomical structures. The method employs a teacher-student architecture with a shared diffusion encoder to learn domain-invariant feature representations and separate teacher and student decoders to decouple labeled and unlabeled data, reducing overfitting and improving robustness. To address the severe class imbalance caused by the small size of plaques, we developed a plaque-aware oversampling strategy and a labeled-data-guided training for the shared encoder and student decoder. We used 142 NIH non-contrast CT scans, divided into 119 training scans and 23 validation scans. We externally evaluated the method on 95 scans from the University of Wisconsin and 50 scans from Medipol University Mega Hospital and compared its performance with supervised nnU-Net and a strong SSL baseline. RESULTS: The improved SSL method significantly outperformed the original SSL method and supervised training with the same architecture when using 14 labeled training scans ( p < 0.0001  ). With these 14 labeled training scans, it achieved DSC values of 58.8% and 82.3% on CTRATE and Renal Donor, respectively, within 2.7--2.8 percentage points of the same architecture trained with all 119 training scans labeled. CONCLUSION: The SSL method segments plaques in the carotid, aortic, and iliac arteries with performance approaching that of fully supervised training while using only 14 labeled training scans, supporting scalable plaque burden assessment.
